messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 72-year-old African American man who served for decades with the United States Coast Guard and who presented for psychological assessment following a period of escalating distress that his wife of forty-one years described as having "stolen the man I knew." He is a broad-shouldered, deliberate speaker who chose his words carefully during intake, pausing often, as though testing the ground before each step. His PCL-5 score of 76 places him in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across the first several sessions was one of a man whose inner life has been reorganised almost entirely around a single catastrophic afternoon.

Approximately three years ago, Kwame was part of a Coast Guard response team dispatched to a commercial vessel that had reported a chemical emergency in a coastal industrial channel. What began as a routine boarding became something else within minutes. The hold of the vessel contained ruptured drums of an industrial solvent, and the air inside was thick and acrid in a way that registered as wrong before anyone had named it. Kwame recalled the silence first — the eerie absence of the normal sounds of a working ship, no engine hum, no voices from below — and then the burning in his throat, the sudden weight in his chest, the way his vision began to blur at the edges. Two of his crew members collapsed before anyone could reach them. He was pulled from the hold by a colleague and evacuated by helicopter, semi-conscious. He spent eleven days in hospital, and the two men who had gone below before him did not survive.

In the months that followed, Kwame's memories of that afternoon refused to remain in the past. They returned not as vague impressions but with a photographic precision that disturbed him — he could see the exact pattern of condensation on the drum nearest to him, the particular angle of the light through a porthole, as though his mind had taken still images and then strung them into a film that ran on a loop without his permission. When the memory surfaced, it arrived with such emotional force that he would have to stop whatever he was doing — put down his coffee, leave the room, grip the edge of a counter — because the feeling of being overwhelmed was total and immediate. These intrusive replays began to reshape how Kwame understood himself and his world. He had come to believe, with quiet certainty, that he could not manage even minor disturbances — a raised voice on television, a neighbour's car alarm, anything unexpected — because the memory had shown him what he was capable of feeling, and he was certain he could not survive that feeling again. The world, he told his clinician, was not the place he had once thought it was; it was a place where invisible things could kill you before you understood what was happening.

This conviction — that danger is always present and always silent — has become the lens through which Kwame reads his daily environment. He remains on active administrative duty with the Coast Guard, and it is at work, reviewing incident logs and sitting in briefings about maritime hazards, that the threat monitoring becomes most acute. A room that grows suddenly quiet, a pause in a colleague's sentence, the particular stillness before someone delivers bad news — these silences carry the same sensory signature as the hold of that vessel, and his body responds accordingly: heart rate climbing, jaw tightening, a metallic taste at the back of his throat. This physical reactivity then drags the memory forward again, the film resuming mid-frame, and the cycle closes around him. Even at home, where his wife has worked to create calm, Kwame cannot fully lower his guard. He moves through his own house as though something may yet be found in it.

He has not spoken to his wife about the content of the memories, partly because he believes that engaging with them directly — even in words — will breach some internal containment he is barely maintaining. What frightened him most, he admitted in their third session, was not the memory itself but what it proved: that the world offers no real warning, and that he, a man who had spent a career reading the sea, had not seen it coming.

It was his wife who finally made the appointment. Kwame came because he was tired of standing guard inside his own life, and because some part of him, however small, was hoping to be told there was still a way back.
